segments.text: <curious>How do you count something enormous without ever writing out the list? That single question is what this whole chapter answers, and it starts from one clean idea.
Picture a small thali counter near a railway station. You pick one sabzi from four, one roti from three, one sweet from two. The owner says many plates are possible, and we want the exact number.

Here is the key move. Whatever sabzi you take, all three rotis are still open; and for every sabzi and roti pair, both sweets are still there. So the counts do not add, they stack up by multiplying: four times three times two, which is twenty four distinct thalis.
That stacking is the Multiplication Principle, the heart of the Fundamental Principle of Counting. When you make a sequence of independent choices, you multiply the number of options at each stage.

See it as a tree growing left to right. Four branches for the sabzis, each splitting into three for the rotis, each splitting again into two for the sweets. The leaves on the far right are the complete thalis, and counting leaves is just multiplying the branching numbers.
The trigger word is AND. Sabzi and roti and sweet, do this and then that, means the choices combine, and combining means multiply.

Why not just list everything? Because lists explode. A six character password built from letters and digits has over two billion settings. The genius here is that you get the size of the collection while staying blissfully ignorant of its members.
Now change the story a little. The owner says: today take either one of four sabzis or one of two sweets, but not both. This is a completely different situation from before.
You are no longer building a plate stage by stage. You make a single choice from one pile or from the other, and the two piles do not mix.
So you do not multiply here, you add: four sabzi options or two sweet options give four plus two, which is six ways in total. This is the Addition Principle.
The signal word has changed from AND to OR. OR means alternatives, one route instead of the other, and alternatives are added together.
So the whole distinction lives in two tiny English words. AND, do this and then that, combines the choices, so you multiply. OR, do this or instead that, gives alternatives, so you add.

One warning that examiners love. Addition only works when the options are mutually exclusive, with no overlap. If the two piles share a member, naive adding counts it twice, and you must subtract the overlap back later.
So before touching any numbers, translate the problem into ANDs and ORs. That single reading decides whether you reach for multiply or for add.
Where does the factorial come from? Suppose you line up five different trophies on a shelf, and you want to know how many orders are possible.

The first position can be filled by any of the five trophies; the next by any of the remaining four; then three; then two; then the last one. This is a pure multiplication principle chain: five times four times three times two times one, which is one hundred twenty.
That descending product of natural numbers turns up so often that mathematicians gave it a shorthand.
We write it as five factorial, with an exclamation mark, and it equals one hundred twenty. So a factorial is simply the multiplication principle applied to a full arrangement.
In general, n factorial is n times n minus one, times n minus two, all the way down to one. Keep the meaning in your head, not just the symbol: it counts the orders of n distinct things.
<whisper>Here is a definition that surprises everyone: zero factorial equals one, not zero. We will justify that properly in a moment, so do not just memorise it.
And a boundary rule: factorial is defined only for non-negative integers. You cannot take the factorial of a negative number or a fraction at this level.
Let me put your foundation formulas on one board, so you can reach for the right one instantly.
First, the multiplication principle for a chain of stages: m one times m two, up to m k. This is the AND situation, where every stage combines with the next.
Second, the addition principle: m plus n. This is the OR situation, for mutually exclusive alternatives.
Third, the factorial: n factorial is n times n minus one, down to one, with zero factorial defined as one.
Fourth, and this is the identity you will use most, the recursion: n factorial equals n times n minus one factorial. It lets you peel off one factor at a time.
Fifth, counting with repetition. If r slots are each filled independently from the same n options, the count is n to the power r, because every slot sees the full n options afresh.

Keep three structures straight, because the whole chapter forks between them. Repetition allowed gives n to the r. No repetition with order gives a falling product. Arranging all n distinct objects gives n factorial.

One sanity habit: factorials grow ferociously. Five factorial is only one hundred twenty, but ten factorial is over three point six million. So if an exam answer comes out as, say, twenty factorial, you leave it as twenty factorial rather than computing it.
The multiplication principle is not a theorem pulled from thin air, and an examiner rewards you for justifying it. So let us see exactly why it is true.
Think of the task as filling two boxes, left to right, and watch how the choices fan out.
Box one can be filled in m ways. Now fix any one of those choices. With that locked, box two can still be filled in n ways, and crucially this n is the same no matter which box one option you fixed.

So each of the m box-one choices spawns exactly n complete outcomes. Grouping the outcomes by their box-one choice gives m groups of n each, which is m times n, with none missed and none double-counted.
The fine print is that independence assumption: box two's count must not depend on which option box one used. Hold onto that, because it is exactly where harder problems set traps.

The same box-filling argument derives the factorial. Treat the n positions as n boxes: position one takes any of n objects, position two any of the remaining n minus one, and so on down to one. Multiply, and you get n factorial.

It even pins down zero factorial. The recursion says one factorial equals one times zero factorial, which forces zero factorial to be one. And by meaning, there is exactly one way to arrange nothing, the empty arrangement.

board_events.text: The trap: a later stage depends on an earlier choice
Form 3-digit numbers, all digits distinct, from {0,1,2,3}. No leading zero.
Reflex $4\times3\times2=24$ is WRONG: slot 1 can't use 0.
Fix the constrained slot FIRST: slot 1 in 3 ways (digits 1, 2, 3).
Now slots 2 and 3 draw from the 3 remaining digits, which now include 0.
Rule: reorder so the constrained stage is first, or split into cases and add.
Example 1 (CBSE): ID codes
Code = one letter (A-Z) then three digits (0-9), digit repetition allowed.
Example 2: breakfast order (AND vs OR)
Either one ready plate (3) OR a combo of one paratha (4) AND one chutney (5).
Bracket each AND-group with $\times$, then join alternatives with $+$.
Example 3 (JEE Main): even 4-digit numbers, repetition allowed
Handle constrained slots first: thousands $\ne 0$; units must be even.
Example 4 (JEE Adv): 5-digit numbers with at least one 9
"At least one" $\to$ count the complement.
The mistakes that cost marks here
Confusing AND with OR. Translate to AND/OR first, THEN assign $\times$ or $+$.
Assuming 'no repetition' by default. Locks, plates, passwords usually allow it: $n^r$.
Leading digit can face two exclusions at once ($\ne 0$ and $\ne 9 \to 8$, not 9).
Treating $0!$ as 0. It is 1, or later combination formulas collapse.
Adding overlapping OR-cases. Mutually exclusive only, else you double-count the overlap.
Pro-tip: 'at least one' $\to$ Total $-$ none.

segments.text: The multiplication principle has one piece of fine print, and Advanced problems live in the gap when it fails. Let me show it breaking.
Form three-digit numbers with all digits distinct, using the set zero, one, two, three, and no leading zero is allowed.
The reflex answer, four times three times two equals twenty four, is wrong. The first slot cannot use zero, so its count is not the same as the later slots, and the clean symmetry is gone.
The fix is to handle the constrained slot first. Slot one can be one, two, or three, so it has three ways, not four.
Once slot one is chosen, slots two and three draw from the three remaining digits, and those now include zero because the leading rule no longer applies here.
So the count is three, times three times two, which is three times six, giving eighteen, not twenty four.

The general lesson: when a stage's options depend on an earlier choice, either reorder so the constrained stage comes first, or split the problem into disjoint cases and add them. Casework plus the counting principle together handle essentially every problem you will meet.
Let us cash out the theory on two clean examples. First, a CBSE-level one about ID codes.
A school issues codes made of one letter from A to Z, followed by three digits from zero to nine, and digit repetition is allowed. We fill four slots in order.

The letter slot has twenty six ways; each of the three digit slots has ten ways. By the counting principle we multiply: twenty six times ten times ten times ten, which is twenty six thousand codes. Notice the clean rhythm: identify slots, count each, multiply, state the answer.
The second example mixes AND and OR, which is exactly the trap this chapter is built to catch.
A canteen lets you either take a single ready plate, of which there are three, or build a combo of one paratha from four types and one chutney from five types.

The combo is paratha and chutney, an AND, so we multiply to get four times five, which is twenty. The overall order is ready plate or combo, mutually exclusive, so we add: three plus twenty, giving twenty three ways.

A panicking student multiplies everything to get sixty, or adds everything to get twelve. Both ignore the AND-OR structure. The mechanical fix is to bracket each AND group with a times sign, then join the independent alternatives with a plus.
Now two harder examples, both about digit constraints. The reflex to build here is: handle the most constrained slot first.
Example three asks how many four-digit numbers are even, with digit repetition allowed. Two constraints bite at once: the thousands place cannot be zero, and the units place must be even.

So the thousands place has nine ways, from one to nine; the units place has five ways, from zero, two, four, six, eight; and the hundreds and tens each have all ten digits. These are independent, so multiply: nine times ten times ten times five, which gives four thousand five hundred even numbers.
Example four is JEE Advanced. How many five-digit numbers contain the digit nine at least once, no leading zero, repetition allowed?

Counting at least one nine directly means adding the cases of exactly one, two, three, four, or five nines, watching for overcounting. The clean route is the complement: all five-digit numbers minus those with no nine at all.

All five-digit numbers: first digit from one to nine is nine ways, the other four from zero to nine is ten each, giving ninety thousand. Numbers with no nine: the first digit drops both zero and nine, leaving eight ways; each other digit drops only nine, leaving nine ways, giving eight times nine to the fourth, which is fifty two thousand four hundred eighty eight.

<whisper>Here is the subtle point that Advanced loves. The leading digit obeys two exclusions at once, not zero and not nine, so it has eight, while interior digits obey only one and have nine. Subtracting gives ninety thousand minus fifty two thousand four hundred eighty eight, which is thirty seven thousand five hundred twelve.
Let me close the subtopic with the mistakes that quietly cost marks, so you can spot them in yourself.

The most frequent error is confusing AND with OR: multiplying mutually exclusive alternatives, or adding sequential stages. Always translate the words into ANDs and ORs first, and only then assign a times or a plus.

The second is assuming no repetition by default. Many students reflexively write falling products. But locks, number plates, and passwords usually allow repetition, which is n to the r, not a falling product. That fork decides everything.

Third, forgetting boundary constraints. In digit problems the leading digit usually cannot be zero, and it can face two exclusions at once, such as not zero and not nine, which leaves eight options, not nine. Slot the most constrained position first.
Fourth, mishandling zero factorial. It is one, never zero. Treating it as zero collapses the combination formulas you will meet soon into nonsense.

Fifth, adding overlapping OR-cases. The addition principle needs the cases to be mutually exclusive. If your two piles share members, naive addition double-counts, and you must subtract the overlap back.

<whisper>And the pro-tip worth gold: whenever you see the words 'at least one', do not grind through casework. Compute total minus none. It turns a messy sum into two clean products almost every time.

board_events.text: A permutation = arranging objects in a DEFINITE order.
100m podium: Ravi-Meera-Sory is a DIFFERENT result from Meera-Ravi-Sory.
The one word to tattoo on your brain: ORDER MATTERS.
Contrast: picking 3 for a study group. Ravi-Meera-Sory = Meera-Ravi-Sory. Order irrelevant.
List all orders of A, B, C: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA. Exactly six, none repeated.
Permutation = positions. Combination = committee.
Recognising the flavour is half the battle.
1) All distinct, no repetition (medal podium). Counted by ${}^{n}P_r$.
2) Repetition allowed (PIN, number plate). Every slot sees all n: $n^r$.
3) Some objects identical (SAMOSA). Swapping the two S's makes no new word: divide out.
4) Arranged in a circle (round table). Rotate one seat and it's the same: $(n-1)!$
Spot the flavour FIRST; the correct formula then follows.
A curved row of bolted-down chairs is still linear, not circular. Don't be fooled.
Your permutation toolkit
Bridge to combinations: ${}^{n}P_r = r! \cdot {}^{n}C_r$.
Sanity: ${}^{n}P_r$ is always a positive integer; a fractional answer means you erred.
Why ${}^{n}P_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$

segments.text: In the last subtopic you learned to count outcomes. A permutation is one supremely common kind of counting: arranging objects in a definite order.

Picture the medal ceremony after a hundred metre final. If Ravi, Meera, and Sory take gold, silver, and bronze, that is a different outcome from Meera, Ravi, and Sory, even though the same three people are involved. The positions are distinguishable.
That is the soul of a permutation, and it is the one word to tattoo on your brain: order matters. Rearranging the same objects produces a brand new arrangement.

Now contrast it with picking three students to form a study group. Here Ravi, Meera, Sory is the same group as Meera, Ravi, Sory. Order is irrelevant, and that second kind of counting is a combination, which is the next subtopic.
See it with tiny numbers. List every arrangement of the three letters A, B, C taken all at a time: A B C, A C B, B A C, B C A, C A B, C B A.
That is exactly six of them, and not one is a repeat, because six is three factorial. Notice A B C and A C B are counted separately: same letters, different order, different permutation.

So carry one line into everything that follows. Permutation means positions; combination means committee. Getting that distinction firm now saves you from the single most common error in the whole chapter.
Permutations come in a few important flavours, and recognising which one you are in is genuinely half the battle.
Flavour one: all objects distinct, no repetition. This is the medal podium, where each object is used at most once and every position differs. It is counted by n permute r.

Flavour two: repetition allowed, like a PIN or a number plate, where the same digit can reappear. Here every slot sees all n options afresh, giving n to the r. That is the counting principle result from the last subtopic, now living inside permutations.

Flavour three: some objects are identical, like arranging the letters of the word SAMOSA. Swapping the two S's does not create a new word, so we must divide out that redundancy, and plain n permute r no longer applies.

Flavour four: arranged in a circle, like guests around a round dining table. Rotating everyone one seat over gives the same arrangement, so the circle quietly removes one degree of freedom, and the count is n minus one factorial.
The discipline is simple. Spot the flavour first, and the correct formula follows almost automatically. Mixing up the flavour is where most marks are lost.

One honest warning: a curved row of chairs bolted to the floor is still a straight line for our purposes. It only counts as circular if rotating the whole arrangement genuinely gives the same seating.
Let me lay the permutation formulas on one board so you can grab the right one at a glance.
The headline: n permute r equals n times n minus one, down to n minus r plus one, which compresses to n factorial over n minus r factorial, valid for r between zero and n.
Keep the special cases handy. n permute n is n factorial, n permute zero is one, and n permute one is just n.
When repetition is allowed, drop the falling product and use n to the r, because every slot sees all n options again.
When the objects are not all distinct, with p alike of one kind, q of another, and so on, divide n factorial by p factorial, q factorial, and each look-alike group's factorial.
For a circular arrangement of all n objects the count is n minus one factorial; and if the circle can be flipped over, like a necklace or a key-ring, divide by a further two.
Store one bridge for later: n permute r equals r factorial times n choose r. Arranging equals selecting and then ordering, and this single identity ties the two halves of the chapter together.
And a sanity check to lean on: n permute r is always a positive integer for valid r. If your permutation count ever comes out as a fraction, you have made a slip somewhere.
This is a board-favourite derivation, so let us build n permute r from the counting principle, step by step.
We want the number of ways to fill r ordered positions using n distinct objects, with no repetition. Treat the positions as a row of boxes.

Position one can take any of the n objects. Position two can take any object except the one already used, so n minus one. Position three has n minus two, and so on, until position r, where r minus one objects are gone, leaving n minus r plus one.
Multiplying by the counting principle gives n times n minus one, times n minus two, all the way to n minus r plus one. That falling product is the raw form of n permute r.
To compress it into a clean formula, multiply and divide by the missing tail, which is n minus r factorial, the product of everything below n minus r plus one down to one.
The numerator now runs all the way from n down to one, which is simply n factorial, over n minus r factorial. So n permute r equals n factorial over n minus r factorial.
Read what just happened: this whole result is nothing but the counting principle applied to r ordered slots, with the tail folded in to make the algebra tidy.
Two of the four flavours need a correction to the plain factorial, and both come from the same idea: over-counting.

Take the alike-objects case first. Pretend, for a moment, that the p identical objects are secretly labelled, so all n are distinct. Then there are n factorial arrangements. But those labels are invisible.

The p identical objects can be shuffled among themselves in p factorial ways without changing the visible arrangement, so every real arrangement has been counted p factorial times. Divide it out, and with several repeated groups you divide by each group's factorial.
Now the circle, with a concrete check on the board: three friends X, Y, Z around a round table.

Take any one circular seating and read it off starting from each person in turn. That produces n different linear strings, yet they all describe the same circle, because rotating the table reseats no one. So each circle maps to exactly n linear arrangements.

There are n factorial linear arrangements in total, so the number of circles is n factorial over n, which is n minus one factorial. For three friends that predicts two, and indeed only two genuinely different circles exist.
One last twist: if a mirror flip counts as the same, like a necklace or a key-ring turned over, each circle is double counted, so you divide by a further two.
Restricted permutations look scary but reduce to three reflexes. Learn them once and they cover almost every exam variant.
First reflex, must be together: glue the objects that must stay together into a single block, arrange that block among the others, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the block.

Concretely, arrange A, B, C, D, E in a row with A and B together. Glue them as one block, giving four units, arranged in four factorial, which is twenty four ways; the block itself flips in two factorial, that is two ways; so twenty four times two is forty eight.
Second reflex, must not be together: seat all the other objects first. They create gaps, including the two ends, and you drop the restricted objects into separate gaps.

For the same five letters with A and B apart, seat C, D, E first in three factorial, that is six ways, creating four gaps. Place A and B into two of those four gaps in four permute two, which is twelve. Six times twelve is seventy two. And notice forty eight plus seventy two equals one hundred twenty, which is five factorial, the total. Together and not-together must partition everything.
That partition check is the honesty test that catches errors, so use it whenever you can.
Third reflex, a fixed position: lock the constrained object in place first, then freely permute whatever remains. Constraints handled first, freedom last.
And carry forward the bridge that unifies the chapter: n permute r equals r factorial times n choose r. A permutation is simply a combination that has then been put in order.

segments.text: Let us convert the theory into two clean worked examples, one straight and one a classic trap.
Example one, CBSE level. A club has eight members, and we must fill the distinct posts of President, Secretary, and Treasurer, with no member holding two.
Three distinct posts mean order matters, so this is eight permute three. That is eight factorial over five factorial, which is eight times seven times six, giving three hundred thirty six ways.
Example two is a conceptual trap: count the distinct arrangements of all the letters of the word SAMOSA.
First scan for repeats. The letters are S, A, M, O, S, A, so six letters in all, with S appearing twice and A appearing twice, while M and O appear once each.

If all six were distinct, the answer would be six factorial, which is seven hundred twenty. But the two S's are interchangeable, so divide by two factorial, and the two A's likewise, so divide by another two factorial. Six factorial over two factorial times two factorial is seven hundred twenty over four, which is one hundred eighty.

The trap is writing six factorial equals seven hundred twenty and stopping, forgetting that swapping the identical letters produces no new word. Always scan for repeats before reaching for a factorial.
Two more examples, both stitching a constraint onto a permutation. The reflex, as always, is to handle the most constrained slot first.
Example three, JEE Main. Using the digits one to five without repetition, how many four-digit even numbers can we form? The word even pins down the units place, so we settle that first.

The units digit must be even, so it comes from the set two, four, giving two choices. The remaining three positions are filled from the four unused digits with order mattering, which is four permute three, equal to twenty four.
Multiply: two times twenty four is forty eight even four-digit numbers. The parity restriction fixed one slot, and n permute r arranged the rest.
Example four is a lovely JEE Advanced one: seat five boys and three girls around a circular table so that no two girls sit next to each other.

Build it in the order that respects the constraint. Seat the boys first, and since it is circular, that is five minus one factorial, which is twenty four. The five seated boys create five gaps between them.

To keep the girls apart, each girl goes into a separate gap. Choosing and ordering three girls into five gaps is five permute three, equal to sixty. So the total is twenty four times sixty, which is one thousand four hundred forty.

The rigorous move is anchoring the unconstrained group first. Seating the girls directly would tangle the no-adjacency condition into the circular count; seating boys first turns the restriction into a clean gap-filling step. That is the circular gap method.
Let me close permutations with the mistakes that quietly leak marks, so you can catch them in your own working.

The big one is order confusion: using n permute r when order does not actually matter, where you really wanted n choose r. Always run the master test. If you swap two chosen objects, is it a new outcome? Yes means permutation; no means combination.
Second, forgetting to divide for alike objects, that is writing n factorial for a word with repeated letters. Always scan for repeats and quotient them out.

Third, circular slips. Using n factorial instead of n minus one factorial for a round arrangement, or forgetting the extra divide by two for necklaces, bracelets, and key-rings that can be flipped over.
Fourth, the repetition fork. Defaulting to n permute r when the problem actually allows repetition. That case is n to the r, not a falling product.

For restrictions, keep the two reflexes crisp. For together, glue the group into one block, arrange, then multiply by the block's internal arrangements. For not together, seat everyone else first and drop the restricted items into the gaps.
<whisper>And the one that saves the most time on a circle: fix one object to kill the rotational symmetry, and the whole problem collapses to a familiar linear one on the remaining objects.

segments.text: In the last subtopic order was everything. A combination is the mirror image: you only select a group of objects, and order is completely irrelevant.

Picture the selectors of a cricket squad choosing eleven players from a pool of sixteen. Once the eleven names are down, it makes no difference whether a selector wrote them top to bottom or in any other sequence. The team is the same set of eleven people.
So the watchword flips. In permutations it was order matters; in combinations it is order does not matter. If you shuffle the chosen objects and get nothing new, you are looking at a combination.
See it with pairs on the board. From four objects A, B, C, D the selections of size two are A B, A C, A D, B C, B D, C D, exactly six of them, because A B and B A are the same pair, not two.

This is why handshakes among nine people number nine choose two, which is thirty six, and not nine permute two, which is seventy two. A shakes with B and B shakes with A are the same handshake, so we strip that order away.

That gives the whole idea in one line: a combination is a permutation with the ordering stripped off. You take n permute r and divide by r factorial, the number of ways the chosen group could be reordered.
So keep the test sharp. Selection alone is a combination. Selection plus roles, ranks, or positions is a permutation, and it costs you the extra r factorial.
Let me put the combination formulas on one board. They are all examinable, so learn to read them fluently.
The core: n choose r equals n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial, which also equals n permute r divided by r factorial, valid for r between zero and n.
The boundaries: n choose zero and n choose n are both one, n choose one is n, and n choose r is zero whenever r exceeds n, since you cannot choose more objects than exist.
The symmetry property, and it is the most useful one: n choose r equals n choose n minus r. Choosing which r to keep is the same act as choosing which n minus r to reject.

segments.text: Two worked examples now, and the second is the single most tested discrimination in the chapter.

Example one, CBSE level. A cricket squad has eleven players, and we choose a sub-committee of four to meet the coach. A sub-committee is a plain selection, the order of the four names is irrelevant, so we use eleven choose four.

That is eleven times ten times nine times eight, over four times three times two times one. The top is seven thousand nine hundred twenty, the bottom is twenty four, and the answer is three hundred thirty.

Example two puts permutation and combination side by side. From six eligible students, count two things: first choose three for a quiz team, then appoint three to the distinct posts of leader, scribe, and timekeeper.
The team is order irrelevant, so it is six choose three, which is twenty. The posts are distinct, so order matters, and that is six permute three, which is one hundred twenty.

Notice one hundred twenty equals twenty times three factorial. The appointments are simply the teams with the three factorial internal orderings restored. Students who do not pause to ask does the chosen group have roles will use a permutation for a plain selection, overcounting by r factorial, or a combination for a role assignment, undercounting.

Two more examples, showing how AND-multiply and the at-least pattern play out inside combinations. Example three is JEE Main: form a committee of four from seven boys and five girls, with exactly two boys and two girls.
The two choices are independent, joined by an AND, so we multiply, exactly the reflex from the very first subtopic.

Choose two boys from seven, which is seven choose two, equal to twenty one; choose two girls from five, which is five choose two, equal to ten. Multiply to get twenty one times ten, which is two hundred ten.
Example four is JEE Advanced. From eight men and six women, form a committee of five containing at least three women.
At least three women, in a committee of five, allows three, four, or five women. These cases are mutually exclusive, so count each and add.

Three women and two men is six choose three times eight choose two, twenty times twenty eight, which is five hundred sixty. Four women and one man is six choose four times eight choose one, fifteen times eight, which is one hundred twenty. Five women and no men is six choose five times eight choose zero, which is six.
Adding the three cases gives five hundred sixty plus one hundred twenty plus six, which is six hundred eighty six.

Here the complement, zero, one, or two women, is also three cases, so it saves nothing. Complementary counting wins only when the complement is genuinely shorter, and spotting which route is shorter is the Advanced-level judgement being tested.
Let me close combinations with the mistakes that quietly leak marks, and the two pro-tips that recover them.

The cross-cutting error is order confusion: using n choose r when the problem assigns roles or positions, which needs n permute r, or the reverse, using n permute r for a plain selection. Always run the master test: would reshuffling the chosen objects create a new outcome?
Closely related is forgetting to divide by r factorial: computing n permute r when n choose r was wanted, so the answer comes out exactly r factorial times too large.
Third, mishandling at least or at most, either by missing a case in the sum, or by reaching for the complement when it is not actually shorter. Count the cases on each side first, then pick.

Fourth, grouping without de-labelling: when dividing objects into equal, unlabelled groups, you must divide by the factorial of the number of equal groups, or you over-count the swaps between identical-sized groups.
The first pro-tip is symmetry: use n choose r equals n choose n minus r to shrink the arithmetic. Fifty choose forty eight becomes fifty choose two in a single line.

<whisper>And the second, worth its weight in gold: for constraint problems, deploy the Pascal-style question, is this specific object in or out, to break the count into clean, addable cases every time.

segments.text: So far you have always chosen exactly r objects. Real problems ask broader questions, and this subtopic builds three tools that answer them.
How many subsets are there altogether? In how many ways can identical sweets be shared? How many integer solutions does an equation have? Three tools, one for each.
Start with the picture on the board. Stand in front of n distinct objects and, for each one, make a decision: take it, or leave it.
That is tool one. Each object independently offers two choices, take or leave, so by the counting principle the number of outcomes is two to the n.
So an n-element set has two to the n subsets, counting the empty one. If you must take at least one object, just drop that empty selection, giving two to the n minus one.
The clean way to see it is that a selection is a binary string of length n: a one wherever an object is in, a zero wherever it is out. There are two to the n such strings.

One honest caution the exam exploits. This picture is for distinct objects. If you have p identical chocolates, a selection only records how many you take, anything from zero to p, which is p plus one choices, not two to the p. Handle alike groups separately.
Tool two handles a case the earlier formulas do not: selection with repetition. You choose r items from n types, repeats are allowed, and order does not matter.
Be clear this is neither of the old formulas. It is not n choose r, because repeats are allowed, and it is not n to the r, because order is ignored. It needs its own model.
Here is the clever model. Lay down r identical stars, one for each item you pick, and separate them into n type-groups using n minus one bars.

Every arrangement of stars and bars is exactly one valid selection: the stars before the first bar are type one, those between the first and second bar are type two, and so on. So you are simply choosing which n minus one of the r plus n minus one positions hold the bars.
Tool three is about a distinction that trips people constantly: grouping versus distribution.
Divide twelve books into three bundles, and give twelve books to three children, sound almost the same, but they differ by whether the groups are labelled.

That single feature drives the arithmetic. Unlabelled equal-size groups force a division by the number of such groups factorial, while labelled recipients, being distinct, do not. Converting between the two is a frequent exam pivot.
Here is the full toolkit for this subtopic on one board. Six formulas, and the trick is matching the situation to the right one.
Subsets of n distinct objects: two to the n, including the empty set, or two to the n minus one if you need at least one.
When some objects are alike, with p of one kind, q of another, and d genuinely distinct ones, the total is p plus one, times q plus one, and so on, times two to the d.
Choosing r from n types with repetition, order ignored, is n plus r minus one choose r, which equals n plus r minus one choose n minus one. That is stars and bars.
For integer solutions of x one plus up to x k equals n, the non-negative count is n plus k minus one choose k minus one, and the strictly positive count is n minus one choose k minus one.

To divide n distinct objects into groups of sizes m one, m two, and so on, use n factorial over the product of those factorials, then divide by g factorial for each set of g equal-sized unlabelled groups.
And placing n distinct objects into k distinct boxes with no restriction is simply k to the n.
One master move to store: whenever every box must get at least one, give one to each box first, then solve the leftover as a clean non-negative stars-and-bars problem.
The stars-and-bars formula deserves a proper proof, because once you see it, a whole family of hard-looking problems becomes one line.
Look at the board. We are selecting r items from n types, repetition allowed, order irrelevant, and we represent the selection with r identical stars laid in a line.

Now partition those stars into n type-blocks by inserting n minus one bars. The stars before the first bar belong to type one, those between the first and second bar to type two, and so on down the line.

Every distinct selection corresponds to exactly one star-and-bar pattern, and every pattern to one selection. We have r plus n minus one symbols in total, and we simply choose which n minus one of those positions are the bars.
That is n plus r minus one choose n minus one, which by symmetry also equals n plus r minus one choose r. The proof is complete.

And notice the twin reading: choosing r from n types with repetition is identical to placing r identical objects into n distinct boxes, which is the same as counting non-negative integer solutions of x one plus up to x n equals r.

For the strictly positive case, where each variable must be at least one, first hand one unit to every variable by setting y i equals x i minus one. That reduces it straight back to the clean non-negative case, and this give-one-to-everybody trick is the master move for lower bounds.
Let us quickly justify the two remaining tools, so they are understanding and not just memory.

For total selections, each of the n distinct objects is independently in or out, two choices each, so the counting principle gives two times two, and so on, which is two to the n. Subtract one to forbid the empty choice.

For an alike group of size p, a selection is fully described by how many you take, anything from zero to p, that is p plus one options. Distinct objects each contribute their own factor of two, and the groups multiply together.
Now the grouping rule, with the picture on the board showing the crucial difference.

To divide n distinct objects, write n factorial over the product of the group-size factorials. Then, for each set of g equal-sized unlabelled groups, divide by g factorial, because relabelling those equal groups produces the same division and would otherwise be over-counted.
But if the groups go to distinct recipients, say named children, the groups are now labelled and genuinely different outcomes, so the divide by g factorial disappears.

So the same six books, asked two different ways, give two different answers. Division into unlabelled groups versus distribution to labelled recipients is a pivot examiners lean on constantly, so read the question carefully.

segments.text: Two examples on total selections, and the second is the classic distinct-versus-alike trap.

Example one, foundational. A gift shop displays five distinct keychains, and we want the number of ways to buy at least one. Each keychain is independently bought or not, giving two to the five, which is thirty two subsets, including buying nothing. Forbid the empty purchase, and the answer is thirty one.
Example two is the trap. A basket holds three identical red apples, two identical green apples, and one orange, and we pick at least one fruit.

Selections from alike groups are counted by how many you take, not which ones. The red apples give zero, one, two, or three, that is four choices; the green give zero, one, or two, three choices; and the single orange is in or out, two choices.
Multiply: four times three times two is twenty four, including the empty basket, so at least one fruit is twenty four minus one, which is twenty three.

The trap is treating all six fruits as distinct, which would give two to the six minus one, that is sixty three. That badly over-counts, because swapping two identical red apples is not a new selection. Always ask which objects are genuinely interchangeable.
Two examples that show stars and bars doing the heavy lifting, first plain, then with a lower bound.

Example three, JEE Main. How many non-negative integer solutions does a plus b plus c plus d equals twelve have? Read it as twelve identical units distributed among four distinct variables, with empty allowed. So n is twelve and k is four.

Stars and bars gives twelve plus four minus one, choose four minus one, which is fifteen choose three. That is fifteen times fourteen times thirteen over six, which works out to four hundred fifty five.
Example four, JEE Advanced. In how many ways can fifteen identical chocolates be distributed among four children so that each child gets at least two?

Use the give-one, or here give-two, trick. Hand each child two chocolates up front, which uses eight, then freely distribute the remaining seven with no restriction. Let y i be the extra each child receives.

Now y one plus y two plus y three plus y four equals seven, non-negative. Stars and bars gives seven plus four minus one, choose four minus one, which is ten choose three, equal to one hundred twenty.

The move that unlocks it is pre-allocating the guaranteed minimum. Subtracting the two-per-child up front converts the bounded problem into the clean non-negative case, and that single manoeuvre dissolves most distribution constraints.
Let me close this subtopic with the mistakes that leak marks, and the one pro-tip that dissolves most distribution problems.

First, distinct versus alike confusion: using two to the n when the objects are actually identical, where you should use the product of p i plus one, or the reverse. Ask whether swapping two of these objects would create a new selection.

Second, the wrong counting model for repetition. Selecting with repetition is n plus r minus one choose r. It is not n choose r, which forbids repetition, and it is not n to the r, which is ordered placement.
The way to lock it in is to recognise the phrase identical items into distinct boxes. Whenever you see that shape, reach for stars and bars.

Third, division versus distribution. Forgetting the divide by g factorial for equal unlabelled groups, or wrongly applying it when the groups are actually labelled recipients. Read whether the groups are named.
Fourth, forgetting the empty case. Both two to the n and the basic stars-and-bars count include choose nothing, or all in one box. Adjust whenever the problem says at least one.

<whisper>And the pro-tip that pays off constantly: for each box at least c, hand out c to every box first, then solve the leftover as a clean non-negative stars-and-bars problem. That one substitution clears almost every lower-bound constraint.

segments.text: <curious>Most questions that look hard in this chapter are not new mathematics at all. They are familiar selections wearing a costume, and the whole skill is learning to see through it.
Take geometry. Given n points with no three on a line, a straight line is simply a choice of two points, and a triangle is a choice of three points. Nothing more.
So the number of lines is n choose two, and the number of triangles is n choose three. The shape is completely determined by which vertices you select.
The only complication is collinear points, shown on the board: a set of points sitting on one common line.

If m of the points are collinear, then all the pairs among them lie on a single line rather than giving many lines, and any three of them form a flat, zero-area triangle rather than a real one. So we correct.
For lines, subtract the m choose two pairs that collapse, then add back the one real line they share. For triangles, simply subtract m choose three, the degenerate ones.
Hold the one-line idea: counting shapes is really counting the vertices that define them, and the formula follows the moment you name the selection.
Divisors wear the same costume. Write a number N as a product of primes, p one to the a one, times p two to the a two, and so on.
Every divisor of N is built by choosing an exponent for each prime, anything from zero up to a i for the prime p i. Those choices are independent.
The board shows it for three hundred sixty: four choices for the power of two, three for the power of three, two for the power of five.
So by the counting principle, the number of divisors is the product a one plus one, times a two plus one, and so on. A divisor is nothing but a selection of exponents.
Two more disguises. Sum of all numbers formed, and rank of a word, are permutation problems viewed through place value and dictionary order respectively.
The key observation for both: in any complete set of arrangements, each digit lands in each place exactly equally often, which lets you total everything without listing a single number.

So the recurring move for this whole subtopic is simple. Name the underlying selection first, points for shapes, exponents for divisors, positions for arrangements, and the formula follows on its own.
Two more named tools round out this subtopic, and examiners reward students who recognise them on sight.
First, derangements. Sometimes every object has a forbidden position, like placing letters into envelopes so that no letter lands in its own correct envelope.
Counting these directly is messy, because you would juggle the cases of exactly one match, two matches, and so on. Derangements instead need inclusion and exclusion, not a plain factorial.
The formula is n factorial times the alternating series: one, minus one over one factorial, plus one over two factorial, and so on, ending with plus or minus one over n factorial.
Memorise the small values, because they appear constantly: D one is zero, D two is one, D three is two, D four is nine, and D five is forty four.
Second, the exponent of a prime p inside n factorial. You count how many numbers up to n are multiples of p, then how many are multiples of p squared, then p cubed, and keep going.

That is Legendre's neat staircase: floor of n over p, plus floor of n over p squared, plus floor of n over p cubed, and so on. As a special case, the number of trailing zeros of n factorial is just the exponent of five.
Here is every application formula gathered on one board. Read it as a menu: recognise the problem type, then pick the matching line.
Geometry: from n points, lines are n choose two and triangles are n choose three; if m points are collinear, subtract m choose two and add one for lines, and subtract m choose three for triangles.
The diagonals of a convex n-gon are n choose two minus n, which simplifies to n times n minus three, over two.
Rectangles from a grid of a horizontal and b vertical lines are a choose two times b choose two, since a rectangle is a choice of two horizontals and two verticals.

For a number written as a product of prime powers, the number of divisors is the product of each exponent plus one, and the sum of divisors is the product of p to the a plus one minus one, over p minus one.
The sum of all numbers formed from n distinct digits is the digit sum, times n minus one factorial, times the repunit, which is ten to the n minus one over nine.
Derangements are n factorial times the alternating reciprocal-factorial sum, and equivalently n minus one, times the sum of the previous two derangements.
The exponent of a prime p in n factorial is the sum of the floors of n over p to the k, and the trailing zeros of n factorial are exactly the exponent of five.
And rank of a word: at each position, sum the smaller unused letters times the factorial of the positions to the right, accumulate, then add one for the word itself.
Let us prove the three most-tested application formulas, because the proofs double as the method for solving the problems.

For geometry, start as if no three points were collinear, giving n choose two lines. Now suppose m points are collinear. Those m points would have contributed m choose two separate lines, but they actually lie on a single line.
So subtract that m choose two and add back one for their shared line. For triangles, any three of the m collinear points make a zero-area triangle, so simply subtract m choose three.

For divisors, a divisor d of N must look like p one to the e one, and so on, with each exponent e i between zero and a i. Choosing each exponent is independent and offers a i plus one values, so by the counting principle the number of divisors is the product of a i plus one.
For the sum of all numbers formed, fix any one digit in the units place. The remaining n minus one digits then permute freely in n minus one factorial ways.
So each digit appears in the units place exactly n minus one factorial times, and by symmetry in every other place too. The contribution to each column is the digit sum times n minus one factorial.
Summing across the columns gives the digit sum, times n minus one factorial, times one plus ten plus up to ten to the n minus one, which is the repunit. That is the whole formula, derived.
Now the three procedural tools: rank of a word, derangements, and Legendre's exponent.

To rank a word of distinct letters, scan left to right. At each position, count how many unused letters are alphabetically smaller than the current letter, multiply by the factorial of the number of positions still to its right, and accumulate. Add one at the end for the word itself.
For derangements, start from all n factorial permutations and subtract those that fix at least one object, using inclusion and exclusion.

Fixing a chosen set of i objects leaves n minus i factorial arrangements, and there are n choose i such sets. The alternating inclusion-exclusion sum then collapses to n factorial times the sum of minus one to the i over i factorial.
For Legendre, among the numbers one to n, exactly floor of n over p are multiples of p. Of those, floor of n over p squared carry a second factor of p, and so on up the powers.
Summing those counts tallies every factor of p exactly once, giving floor of n over p, plus floor of n over p squared, plus more.
<whisper>The exam signal to burn in: whenever you read none correct or no object in its own place, that is a derangement, so reach straight for inclusion-exclusion and never a plain factorial.
Two examples to make the costumes concrete, starting with divisors.
Example one, foundational. How many positive divisors does three hundred sixty have? First factorise it: three hundred sixty is two cubed, times three squared, times five to the one.
Each divisor chooses an exponent for each prime, so the count is three plus one, times two plus one, times one plus one, which is four times three times two, equal to twenty four divisors.
Example two is the collinear trap. There are ten points in a plane, of which four are collinear, and we count the triangles they form.

Without any restriction, any three points make a triangle, so that is ten choose three, which is one hundred twenty. But the four collinear points yield four choose three, that is four, degenerate flat triangles that must be removed.

So the answer is one hundred twenty minus four, which is one hundred sixteen. The trap is writing one hundred twenty and stopping; three collinear points have zero area and are never a triangle, so always scan for collinear subsets and subtract their m choose three.
Two final examples, one on the sum of numbers and one on derangements.
Example three, JEE Main. Find the sum of all four-digit numbers formed using the digits two, three, four, five exactly once each. The board shows the key idea: each digit visits each place equally.

There are four factorial, that is twenty four, such numbers, and each digit occupies each place four minus one factorial, that is six, times. The sum of the digits is two plus three plus four plus five, which is fourteen, and the place-value repunit is one one one one.
So the sum is fourteen times six times one thousand one hundred eleven. Fourteen times six is eighty four, and eighty four times one one one one is ninety three thousand three hundred twenty four.
Example four, JEE Advanced. Five distinct letters go into five addressed envelopes, one per envelope, so that no letter lands in its correct envelope. This is the derangement count D five.

By the formula, D five is five factorial times one, minus one, plus one half, minus one sixth, plus one twenty fourth, minus one over one hundred twenty. The bracket works out to about zero point three six seven, and one hundred twenty times that is forty four.
Cross-check with the recurrence: D five equals four times D four plus D three, which is four times nine plus two, equal to four times eleven, which is forty four. Both routes agree.
Let me close the whole chapter's content with the application pitfalls, plus the one habit that unlocks the entire subtopic.
First, ignoring collinear corrections: writing n choose three for triangles, or n choose two for lines, without subtracting the collinear cases. Always hunt for points or lines in special position.
Second, an incomplete prime factorisation. The divisor formula needs every prime with its full exponent; a single dropped prime silently halves your answer.

Third, the sum-of-numbers slip. Students multiply by n factorial instead of n minus one factorial. Remember it is n minus one factorial, the number of times each digit sits in a fixed place, not n factorial.
Fourth, treating a derangement as a plain factorial or a single subtraction. None-in-place needs the full alternating inclusion-exclusion sum, nothing less.
Fifth, stopping Legendre at the first term. Multiples of p squared, p cubed, and higher each add extra factors, so keep climbing the staircase until the floor is zero.

From subtopic one: AND means multiply across stages, OR means add across mutually exclusive alternatives, factorial is the falling product with zero factorial equal to one, and repetition gives n to the r.
From permutations: n permute r is n factorial over n minus r factorial, alike objects divide out their repeats, and a circle is n minus one factorial, halved again if it can be flipped.
From combinations: n choose r is n factorial over r factorial times n minus r factorial, with the symmetry and Pascal identities you should now know cold.
From selections and stars and bars: two to the n subsets, the alike-group product, and n plus r minus one choose r for selection with repetition, with the non-negative and positive solution counts.

For grouping and distribution: n factorial over the product of group-size factorials, with a divide by g factorial for each set of equal unlabelled groups, and k to the n for distinct objects into distinct boxes.

For geometry and divisors: lines and triangles as n choose two and three, diagonals as n times n minus three over two, rectangles as the product of two-choices, and divisors as the product of exponents plus one.
And the advanced tools: the sum-of-numbers formula, the derangement series, and Legendre's staircase for the exponent of a prime in a factorial.

Last stop: a rapid-recall sheet for the night before the exam. The golden rule sits on top: translate the words first, then compute.
AND combines stages, so multiply; OR joins mutually exclusive alternatives, so add. Get this right and half the chapter falls into place.
If repetition is allowed, think powers, n to the r; if not, think a falling product or n permute r. That fork is decided by the word 'repetition'.
The master discrimination: if order matters it is a permutation, if you only want a group it is a combination. When unsure, ask whether reshuffling makes a new outcome.
Repeated objects in a word? Divide them out. A round arrangement loses one degree, giving n minus one factorial, and a flippable ring loses another half.
Choosing r to keep equals choosing n minus r to reject, so use symmetry to shrink arithmetic. For constraints, either include or exclude specific objects, or take total minus the complement.
See identical items going into distinct boxes, and reach straight for stars and bars, n plus r minus one choose r.
Splitting into equal unlabelled groups, divide by the number of groups factorial; for lower bounds, pre-give every box its minimum, then count the rest.
For the application types, name the selection: shapes are choices of vertices, and a divisor is one exponent chosen per prime.
<whisper>And keep the two rescue moves ready: at least one becomes total minus none, and none correct becomes a derangement, solved by inclusion and exclusion. Go get those marks.
